title: Deployment Strategies & Tuning ⚙️
description: Fine‑tune the rollout process with maxSurge, maxUnavailable, and other strategies.

slides.title: Deployment Strategies 🗺️
slides.content:
# Two built‑in strategies

1. **RollingUpdate** (default) – replace Pods gradually.
2. **Recreate** – kill all existing Pods before creating new ones (causes downtime).

You set it in the spec:
```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
```

We’ll focus on RollingUpdate because it’s the production standard.

slides.title: Tuning RollingUpdate Parameters 🎛️
slides.content:
## maxSurge and maxUnavailable

These control the pace of the rollout:
- **maxSurge**: how many Pods can be created above the desired number during an update. Can be an integer or percentage (default 25%).
- **maxUnavailable**: how many Pods can be unavailable during the update. Also default 25%.

```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
```
This example ensures no downtime (maxUnavailable=0) and allows at most one extra Pod.

quizData.question: If replicas=10, maxSurge=25% and maxUnavailable=25%, how many Pods can be created above the desired count?
quizData.explanation: 25% of 10 is 2.5; Kubernetes rounds up to 3.

slides.title: Zero‑Downtime Deployments ✅
slides.content:
## The magic formula

To ensure no request is dropped, set:
- `maxUnavailable: 0` – no old Pod is killed until a new one is Ready.
- `maxSurge: 1` (or more) – allow an extra Pod to be created so there’s always one available.

Also ensure your Pods have readiness probes, so they don't receive traffic until truly ready.

slides.title: Example: Zero‑Downtime Spec
slides.codeSnippet:
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:v2
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5

quizData.question: True or False: Setting maxUnavailable to 0 alone guarantees zero downtime.
quizData.explanation: You also need readiness probes so new Pods aren't considered available until they can serve traffic.

slides.title: Recreate Strategy 💣
slides.content:
## When you need a clean start

Recreate kills all old Pods before creating new ones. Use it when:
- Your app cannot handle two versions running concurrently (e.g., database schema changes).
- You want a quick, clean cutover.

```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
```

Downside: downtime proportional to Pod startup time.

slides.title: Pausing and Resuming Rollouts ⏯️
slides.content:
## Fine‑grained control

You can pause a rolling update midway:
```bash
kubectl rollout pause deployment/nginx-deploy
```
Kubernetes will stop creating/killing Pods. You can then resume:
```bash
kubectl rollout resume deployment/nginx-deploy
```

Useful for canary deployments (manually verify a few new Pods before proceeding).

slides.title: Pause/Resume Example
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deploy nginx=nginx:1.26
kubectl rollout pause deployment/nginx-deploy
# Wait, check some new Pods
kubectl rollout resume deployment/nginx-deploy

quizData.question: What happens when you pause a rolling update?

options.text: New Pods stop being created, old Pods stop being killed
All Pods are reverted to the old version

quizData.explanation: Pausing freezes the current state of the rollout; you can inspect and then resume.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Check rollout history details
Use `kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> --revision=N` to see the Pod template of a specific revision. Very handy for debugging.
